To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
shared neural circuits for mentalizing about self and others are found in ventromedia prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and the temporo-parietial junction (TPJ).
the neural systems involved in mentalizing about the self and about others are identical, and that these systems include low-level embodied systems.
shared representations of the self and other in mentalizing are distributed across multiple brain regions including the ventromedial PFC, posterior cingulat/precuneus and TPJ.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the brain implements processes involved in mental state attribution.
how humans understand others' mental states and how such processes are implemented by neural circuits.
the question: How do humans understand others' actions and mental states?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
shared mentalizing neural representations are distributed throughout the brain, and that these distributed representations are implemented by identical circuits.

the shared mentalizing representations are the neural circuits that support mentalizing of self and other and the nature of these representations is that they are the integration of low level embodied processes within high level mentalizing processes.

shared representations of self and others are implemented in a distributed neural circuit that includes the frontal operculomotor, anterior insula, primary motor and premotor cortices, and the presupplemental motor area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the shared neural circuits that support mentalizing of self and others may be the same circuits that support embodied simulations of self and others.

the brain uses shared neural circuits for high-level mentalizing about the self and others, and that these circuits are implemented through the interaction of high-level inference-based representations with low-level embodied/simulation-based representations.

mentalizing about the self and others are implemented by the same neural circuits, and the nature of these circuits may be the integration and interaction of low-level embodied/simulation processes with higher level inference-based processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a modular system, but rather a highly integrated one.
shared neural representations of the self and other are not limited to lower level embodied processes but extend to higher level mentalizing processes.
mentalizing about the self and others is implemented in shared brain circuits, and these circuits interact with lower level brain systems that are involved in the embodiment of self-other processes.
